chunks.text: 3 Methods The COAST framework is designed to learn the gene expression patterns at a target spot through explicit interactions with its heterogeneous spatial context (Fig. 1 ). The framework consists of four major components: (1) a feature extractor, (2) context-specific feature modulation, (3) spatio-relational Transformer, and (4) absolute and differential prediction heads. 3.1 Feature Extraction and Context Sampling Let a whole slide image (WSI) be defined as I = { p i } i = 1 N I=\{p_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} , where p i p_{i} is the image patch associated with spot i i and N N is the total number of spots. For a given target spot t t , let x t ∈ ℝ D x_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{D} denote its feature vector, extracted using a pre-trained feature extractor. To effectively capture both the tissue microenvironment and global structure, we sample a context feature set 𝒞 t = { x 1 , … , x K } \mathcal{C}_{t}=\{x_{1},\dots,x_{K}\} containing K K spot features from I I . This context set consists of two distinct subsets: 𝒞 t = 𝒞 L ∪ 𝒞 G \mathcal{C}_{t}=\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{L}}\cup\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{G}} , where 𝒞 L \mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{L}} contains K L K_{\mathrm{L}} local context spot features sampled via k k -nearest neighbors, 𝒞 G \mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{G}} comprises K G K_{\mathrm{G}} global context spot features, and K = K L + K G K=K_{\mathrm{L}}+K_{\mathrm{G}} . To construct 𝒞 G \mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{G}} during training, we randomly sample spot features from I I to enhance robustness and diversity. During inference, we employ a deterministic stratified grid strategy to ensure reproducible and representative context selection. Finally, each context spot x k ∈ 𝒞 t x_{k}\in\mathcal{C}_{t} is associated with a type indicator c k ∈ { 0 , 1 } c_{k}\in\{0,1\} , where 0 and 1 represent local and global types, respectively.

3.2 Context-Specific Modulation and Spatio-Relational Transformer Both target and context spot features are projected into a latent space using a shared encoder head Φ h ​ e ​ a ​ d \Phi_{head} , which consists of a linear layer followed by a LeakyReLU activation and dropout: h t = Φ h ​ e ​ a ​ d ​ ( x t ) , h k = Φ h ​ e ​ a ​ d ​ ( x k ) h_{t}=\Phi_{head}(x_{t}),\quad h_{k}=\Phi_{head}(x_{k}) (1) where h t , h k ∈ ℝ d h_{t},h_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} . Although context spot features are sampled from spatially proximal (local) and distant (global) regions, the individual features x k x_{k} only carry localized visual information, without retaining their spatial context. Accordingly, naively aggregating local and global context with the target spot can conflate heterogeneous signals and weaken type-specific contributions during context integration. To effectively integrate these heterogeneous context sources and resolve this spatial ambiguity, we employ a contextual feature modulation mechanism with two sets of scale ( γ \gamma ) and shift ( β \beta ) parameters: γ 0 , β 0 ∈ ℝ d \gamma_{0},\beta_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} for local context ( c k = 0 c_{k}=0 ) and γ 1 , β 1 ∈ ℝ d \gamma_{1},\beta_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} for global context ( c k = 1 c_{k}=1 ). We learn these context-specific scale and shift parameters via embedding layers to modulate the context features: h ~ k = h k ⊙ ( 1 + γ c k ) + β c k \tilde{h}_{k}=h_{k}\odot(1+\gamma_{c_{k}})+\beta_{c_{k}} (2) where ⊙ \odot denotes element-wise multiplication. This allows the model to adaptively condition the latent representations based on their spatial context type. We then form a token sequence by concatenating the target token and the modulated context tokens, [ h t ; h ~ 1 , … , h ~ K ] [h_{t};\tilde{h}_{1},\dots,\tilde{h}_{K}] , and feed it into a standard L L -layer Transformer encoder to aggregate heterogeneous context.

The Transformer encoder outputs refined context-aware representations Z = [ z t ; z 1 , … , z K ] Z=[z_{t};z_{1},\dots,z_{K}] . 3.3 Absolute and Differential Prediction Heads We project the refined features Z Z using a shared projection head Φ p ​ r ​ o ​ j \Phi_{proj} to obtain the final spot representation f t = Φ p ​ r ​ o ​ j ​ ( z t ) ∈ ℝ D f_{t}=\Phi_{proj}(z_{t})\in\mathbb{R}^{D} and context representations f k = Φ p ​ r ​ o ​ j ​ ( z k ) ∈ ℝ D f_{k}=\Phi_{proj}(z_{k})\in\mathbb{R}^{D} . The projection head Φ p ​ r ​ o ​ j \Phi_{proj} includes a sequence of LN, a linear layer, LeakyReLU, and dropout. To capture both absolute and relative expression patterns, we introduce two independent linear prediction heads: (1) Regression Head ( ϕ r ​ e ​ g \phi_{reg} ): Predicts the absolute gene expression vector y ^ t = ϕ r ​ e ​ g ​ ( f t ) \hat{y}_{t}=\phi_{reg}(f_{t}) and (2) Differential Head ( ϕ d ​ i ​ f ​ f \phi_{diff} ): Predicts the expression difference between the target and each context spot from their feature difference, Δ ​ y ^ t , k = ϕ d ​ i ​ f ​ f ​ ( f t − f k ) \Delta\hat{y}_{t,k}=\phi_{diff}(f_{t}-f_{k}) , for k = 1 , ⋯ , K k=1,\cdots,K . 3.4 Training Objectives The total objective function ℒ \mathcal{L} is defined as the weighted sum of the absolute regression loss ℒ r ​ e ​ g \mathcal{L}_{reg} and the differential regression loss ℒ d ​ i ​ f ​ f \mathcal{L}_{diff} : ℒ = ‖ y t − y ^ t ‖ 2 ⏟ ℒ r ​ e ​ g + w diff ​ 1 K ​ ∑ k = 1 K ‖ Δ ​ y t , k − Δ ​ y ^ t , k ‖ 2 ⏟ ℒ d ​ i ​ f ​ f \mathcal{L}=\underbrace{\|y_{t}-\hat{y}_{t}\|^{2}}_{\mathcal{L}_{reg}}+w_{\mathrm{diff}}\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\underbrace{\|\Delta y_{t,k}-\Delta\hat{y}_{t,k}\|^{2}}_{\mathcal{L}_{diff}} (3) where Δ ​ y t , k = y t − y k \Delta y_{t,k}=y_{t}-y_{k} and y t y_{t} and y k y_{k} are ground-truth expression vectors for the target and context spots, and w diff w_{\mathrm{diff}} is a hyperparameter.

This explicit supervision of relative differences encourages the model to learn stable spatial gradients of gene expression, enhancing robustness against slide-level batch effects. 4 Experiments 4.1 Implementation Details We employed UNI [ 2 ] as a frozen pre-trained feature extractor. COAST used an input hidden dimension D = 1024 D{=}1024 , Transformer L = 3 L{=}3 layers, embedding dimension d = 512 d{=}512 and H = 8 H{=}8 attention heads. We set K L = 18 K_{\mathrm{L}}=18 and K G = 72 K_{\mathrm{G}}=72 ( K = 90 K=90 total) and set the differential weight to w diff = 1.0 w_{\mathrm{diff}}=1.0 . The model was optimized with Adam (learning rate 2 × 10 − 4 2\times 10^{-4} , weight decay 1 × 10 − 4 1\times 10^{-4} ) for 10 epochs with batch size 1, selecting the best checkpoint on validation PCC. In this study, we used seven SpaRED datasets that include predefined test splits and contain 128 target genes: Abalo Human Squamous Cell Carcinoma (AHSCC) [ 1 ] , Erickson Human Prostate Cancer P1 (EHPCP1) [ 4 ] , Mirzazadeh Mouse Bone (MMBO) [ 10 ] , Mirzazadeh Mouse Brain P1 (MMBP1) and P2 (MMBP2) [ 10 ] , Vicari Mouse Brain (VMB) [ 16 ] , and Villacampa Lung Organoid (VLO) [ 17 ] . For each spot, we directly used the provided 224 × 224 224{\times}224 H&E patch and the Transcripts Per Million (TPM) normalized, log1p-transformed expression values released in SpaRED. 4.3 Comparison Results We compared COAST with six representative and competitive baseline models, including STNet, Hist2ST, TCGN, EGNv2, NH2ST, and PEKA. For baseline models, we used the official implementations and followed their default hyperparameter settings. Table 1 summarizes the average performance across seven SpaRED datasets. We report gene-wise averages over G = 128 G=128 genes using Pearson Correlation Coefficient (PCC), Mutual Information (MI) estimated with k-nearest neighbors ( k = 5 k=5 ), ROC-AUC 0vNZ for distinguishing zero from non-zero expression, ROC-AUC Q50 for discriminating values above and below the median, and Normalized Root Mean Square Error (NRMSE). COAST achieved the best performance on all five evaluation metrics, obtaining substantial performance gains over all baselines: 0.0399 ∼ \sim 0.4171 in PCC, 0.0378 ∼ \sim 0.1295 in MI, 0.0059 ∼ \sim 0.1783 in AUC 0vNZ , 0.0291 ∼ \sim 0.2170 in AUC Q50 , and 0.0077 ∼ \sim 0.0716 in NRMSE.

We further analyzed per-dataset performance using radar charts and Top-1 frequency rates, measuring how often a method achieves the best result among all competing models (Fig. 2 ). COAST consistently formed the largest polygons in radar charts and obtained the highest Top-1 frequency, indicating superior and balanced performance across diverse datasets and evaluation metrics. Qualitative assessment via Leiden clustering on reconstructed expression (Fig. 3 ) further reveals that COAST captures more coherent spatial domains, reflecting improved structural consistency. For context sampling, the combination K L = 18 K_{\mathrm{L}}{=}18 and K G = 72 K_{\mathrm{G}}{=}72 yielded the best performance (PCC= 0.4262 0.4262 ), whereas increasing either K L K_{\mathrm{L}} or K G K_{\mathrm{G}} degraded performance. The ablation of w diff w_{\mathrm{diff}} revealed the critical role of differential learning. Removing the differential objective ( w diff = 0 w_{\mathrm{diff}}=0 ) led to a substantial decrease in PCC by 0.0477 0.0477 . While optimal performance was achieved at w diff = 1.0 w_{\mathrm{diff}}{=}1.0 , increasing the weight to 2.0 resulted in a performance drop. Regarding context-specific modulation, jointly applying scaling and shifting ( γ ​ and ​ β \gamma\text{ and }\beta ) achieved the strongest performance. Overall, these results suggest that COAST’s gains are not driven by a single component but arise from complementary design choices.

Across these three experiments, most ablation variants remained superior to PEKA (the strongest baseline), further indicating the superiority of COAST. Patient-level data splits were used with 5-fold cross-validation. Patch-level image features were extracted using the frozen UNI [ 2 ] , and gene expression representations were inferred from a model pretrained on the VLO dataset without fine-tuning. We employed CLAM-SB [ 8 ] for slide-level risk prediction and optimized the model using the Cox proportional hazards partial likelihood [ 3 ] . We compared three input configurations: (1) image features only (Img-Only), (2) image features combined with PEKA-predicted expression representations (Img+PEKA), and (3) image features combined with COAST-predicted expression representations (Img+COAST). For a biological reference, a bulk RNA baseline was trained using a standard Cox proportional hazards model directly on patient-level bulk transcriptomic profiles without image features.

OS prediction performance was quantified using the concordance index (C-index). As shown in Table 3 , Img+COAST achieved an average C-index of 0.6029 0.6029 , comparable to bulk RNA ( 0.6042 0.6042 ) and outperforming Img-Only ( 0.5845 0.5845 ) and Img+PEKA ( 0.5904 0.5904 ). These results demonstrate that COAST-derived representations capture clinically meaningful prognostic signals from morphology alone. Table 3: Results of overall survival (OS) prediction on TCGA-LUAD. By incorporating both local microenvironment and global tissue structure as heterogeneous context spots, COAST effectively overcomes the limitations of existing methods that primarily focused on patch-level regression. Across seven datasets, COAST consistently outperforms representative baselines.

Beyond prediction accuracy, COAST-derived expression representations preserve clinically meaningful prognostic signals, improving OS prediction on TCGA-LUAD when combined with histology features, comparable to actual bulk RNA sequencing data. These findings suggest that context-aware differential learning is an effective strategy for enhancing histology-based spatial gene expression prediction. {credits} 5.0.1 Acknowledgements This work was supported by a grant of the National Research Foundation of Korea (NRF) (No. RS-2025-00558322 and RS-2024-00397293).
